title: High Volume Edge
teaches: The High Volume Edge as we trade it: an up day on record volume in a lesser-known stock with a fresh story, its close (the HVC) marked with a ray and an AVWAP; the buy is day 2's dip under the HVC and trade back over it at market, the stop a few cents under the day-2 low, a third off at 3R and 5R with the rest trailed, and a close under the HVC is not a failure.

facts.quote: Our focus in the HVC setup is not just on any high volume but on the highest volume.
facts.claim: Duncan: the focus is not any high volume but the highest volume.

facts.quote: We ideally want to see the stock closing at 75% or higher of its daily range on the gap day. 50% is usually the lowest end DCR that I’ll trade.
facts.claim: Duncan wants a close at 75% or more of the day's range, 50% at the least.

facts.quote: The closing price of the gap-up day serves as our primary entry point.
facts.claim: Duncan buys the close of the gap-up day.

facts.quote: I typically set a hard stop-loss at 3-5% below the HVC.
facts.claim: Duncan's stop is 3% to 5% under the HVC.

facts.quote: An additional exit criterion is an end-of-day close below the HVC.
facts.claim: Duncan also exits on a close under the HVC.

facts.quote: This pattern occurs after a stock gaps up on huge volume due to earnings or another major news event.
facts.claim: Duncan: the pattern follows a gap on huge volume from earnings or major news.

facts.quote: In many cases the volume on earnings day might be the highest volume in the history of the stock or multi year high volume.
facts.claim: Bonde: the volume on a big earnings day is often the highest in the stock's history.

facts.quote: Earnings breakout on companies with significant analyst coverage do not do as well as the first kinds.
facts.claim: Bonde: earnings breakouts in widely covered companies do not do as well.

facts.quote: Stocks with no analyst coverage are typically smaller companies or companies which are out of favor.
facts.claim: Bonde: stocks with no analyst coverage are smaller or out of favor.

facts.quote: Because we track earnings daily most of the time we enter these kind of trades in pre market or at open.
facts.claim: Bonde enters these trades pre-market or at the open.

facts.quote: I rarely trade in extended hours but prefer to wait for the opening range highs
facts.claim: Kullamagi waits for the opening-range high on the gap day.

facts.quote: We can fix our anchor from meaningful market events, not just fixed time periods.
facts.claim: Shannon anchors a VWAP at a meaningful market event.

facts.quote: is anchored to a large price movement event.
facts.claim: Shannon's example anchors at a large price movement event.

facts.quote: Stop first (by default a few cents under the day's low or the prior day's low, F62); the size comes from the stop; if the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade.
facts.claim: A3: stop first, a few cents under the day's low; the size comes from the stop; if the honest stop does not fit, skip.

facts.quote: The stop is the exit. It only moves up, never down or wider. The one exception is the gap rule (B20).
facts.claim: A4: the stop is the exit; it only moves up, never wider; the gap rule is the one exception.

facts.quote: Shares = account × risk % ÷ (entry − stop), rounded down, then capped: the size is the SMALLER of the risk-based size and the position cap
facts.claim: A5: shares are account times risk percent, divided by entry minus stop, rounded down, then capped.

facts.quote: Move the stop to breakeven at 2R to 5R, ideally. The first trim: the hard rule is a third at 3R; ideally anywhere from 3R to 6R, and in practice he mostly waits for 5R.
facts.claim: B19: breakeven between 2R and 5R; the hard rule for the first trim is a third at 3R.

facts.quote: A gap against the stop: the first 30 minutes of the gap-down day decide. The low of the first 30-minute bar is the new stop.
facts.claim: B20: on a gap through the stop, the first 30-minute low is the new stop.

facts.quote: With a ceiling: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out.
facts.claim: B20's ceiling: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out.

facts.quote: No new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report; hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R.
facts.claim: B22: no new buys in the 3 days before a report; hold through one only if up 5R.

facts.quote: The 200-day line: no longs below the 200-day simple moving average, unless it is a parabolic long; shorts only below the 200-day, never above it unless it is a parabolic short.
facts.claim: B26: no longs below the 200-day simple moving average, except a parabolic long.

facts.quote: No chasing: never buy more than 4% above the buy point.
facts.claim: C28: never buy more than 4% above the buy point.

facts.quote: Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays under the buy point, so the distance grows and the shares shrink (A5).
facts.claim: C28: chasing costs size, because the stop stays put and the distance grows.

facts.quote: Time stop: a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, freeing the money.
facts.claim: C33: a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold.

facts.quote: Every position has a real stop order with the broker, not a stop kept in your head.
facts.claim: D41: a real stop order with the broker.

facts.quote: Never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume; illiquid stocks are not even watched.
facts.claim: D42: never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume.

facts.quote: After the first third at 3R: another third at 5R, then trail the last third; adjustable.
facts.claim: E51: another third at 5R, then trail the last third.

facts.quote: Entries are market orders.
facts.claim: E57: entries are market orders.

facts.quote: No new buys outside regular trading hours.
facts.claim: E58: no new buys outside regular hours.

facts.quote: The stop sits a few cents under the day's low, not exactly on it.
facts.claim: F62: the stop sits a few cents under the day's low.

facts.quote: If a stock opens above a trim level (3R, 5R), take that trim at the open.
facts.claim: F63: a trim level the day opens past is taken at the open.

facts.quote: The market reading as a guide (A10): Green, full risk per grade and up to 10 positions; Yellow, smaller and fewer; Orange, only A+ setups; Red, mostly cash and shorts.
facts.claim: F65: Green full risk; Yellow smaller and fewer; Orange only A+; Red mostly cash and shorts.

facts.quote: After a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade with its own stop and every rule.
facts.claim: B21: after a stop-out, buy again only on a new trigger, as a new trade.

facts.quote: A climax run on your own long (Bracco's parabolic burst): sell a big part into it, a judgment call.
facts.claim: C34: sell a big part into a climax run on your own long.

facts.quote: The full size at one price with one stop; no adding.
facts.claim: A5: full size at one price, one stop, no adding.

facts.quote: No setup, no trade: never force a trade to have something on; cash is a position.
facts.claim: D44: no setup, no trade; cash is a position.

facts.quote: A lesser-known stock, often neglected or beaten down, with no prior trend required. A fresh story arrives all at once.
facts.claim: The context: a lesser-known, often neglected stock; a fresh story arrives all at once.

facts.quote: Its close is the HVC, a level marked with a ray and an AVWAP for months.
facts.claim: The record day's close is the HVC, marked with a ray and an AVWAP.

facts.quote: RED TO GREEN on day 2: the session after the HVE opens at or under the HVC, trades under it, then trades back over it; a market order a cent over the HVC.
facts.claim: The trigger: day 2 opens at or under the HVC, trades under, then back over; buy at market a cent over.

facts.quote: A few cents under the day-2 low, the low made before the reclaim. Never the HVC itself, and never the HVE low on a day-2 entry.
facts.claim: The stop: a few cents under the day-2 low; never the HVC, never the HVE low.

facts.quote: Day 2 reclaims the HVC and closes back under the fill, or the stock slices back under the HVE low within weeks and the level turns into overhead.
facts.claim: The failure mode: a close back under the fill, or a slide under the HVE low that turns the level into overhead.

facts.quote: The trade, not the HVE day, is above the 200-day SMA at the moment of entry.
facts.claim: The trade, not the HVE day, must be above the 200-day at entry.

facts.quote: A fresh story: a contract, a trial result, a partnership, a government stake, an IPO-year re-rating, or earnings so big the volume is extreme. Earnings on ordinary big volume is a PEG, not an HVE.
facts.claim: A fresh story; earnings on ordinary big volume is a PEG, not an HVE.

facts.quote: An up close: the HVE day closes over the prior close. Long only.
facts.claim: The HVE day closes up; long only.

facts.quote: Not these days: the monthly options expiry (the third Friday) and the last session of a month. The volume is not demand.
facts.claim: Never the monthly options expiry or a month's last session.

facts.quote: Not a climax: not after a run of 60% or more in the prior 60 sessions, and not on the third to fifth day of a straight-up burst.
facts.claim: Not after a 60% run in 60 sessions, not on day 3 to 5 of a straight-up burst.

facts.quote: Mark the level: a horizontal ray at the HVC and an anchored VWAP from the HVE day, kept on the chart for months. Later setups form there.
facts.claim: Mark a ray at the HVC and an AVWAP from the HVE day; later setups form there.

facts.quote: The taught trigger is on day 2, the one session after the HVE day. Not the HVE close, not a later day.
facts.claim: The taught trigger is day 2, not the HVE close or a later day.

facts.quote: Day 2 opens at or under the HVC and trades under it. A day 2 that opens over the HVC and never trades under it is not this trigger; it may become a later entry.
facts.claim: Day 2 must open at or under the HVC and trade under it.

facts.quote: Red to green through the HVC: the moment day 2 trades back over the HVE close, buy with a market order a cent over the HVC.
facts.claim: Buy at market a cent over the HVC the moment day 2 trades back over it.

facts.quote: No buy more than 4% over the HVC; the HVC is the buy point.
facts.claim: No buy more than 4% over the HVC.

facts.quote: No buys outside regular trading hours. Bonde buys the event day pre-market; we do not.
facts.claim: No buys outside regular hours; we do not buy pre-market.

facts.quote: the follow-up entries are the house's own setups at the level: an Oops Reversal or an undercut and rally at the HVC, a hold of the 9 or 20 EMA near the HVC, a tight flag over the HVC.
facts.claim: After day 2, later entries are our own setups at the level, each with its own trigger.

facts.quote: Each has its own trigger and stop.
facts.claim: Each later entry has its own trigger and stop.

facts.quote: The HVC itself is never the stop: price trades under it in 98% of cases within 60 sessions
facts.claim: The HVC is never the stop; price trades under it in 98% of cases within 60 sessions.

facts.quote: Full size at one price with one stop; no adding.
facts.claim: One price, one stop, no adding.

facts.quote: Stop to breakeven between 2R and 5R, at the first trim by default.
facts.claim: Breakeven between 2R and 5R, at the first trim by default.

facts.quote: Before the trade: day 2 never trades back over the HVC. No trigger; the chart may give a later entry at the level.
facts.claim: No reclaim on day 2, no trigger.

facts.quote: For the level: a close under the HVE day's low ends it as support. After that the HVC is overhead, not a floor.
facts.claim: A close under the HVE low ends the level as support; the HVC becomes overhead.

facts.quote: Trading or closing under the HVC is not an invalidation of the level. Do not erase it.
facts.claim: Under the HVC is not an invalidation; do not erase the level.

facts.quote: A lesser-known stock: 50-day dollar volume under about $100 million a day before the event. Not a mega-cap.
facts.claim: Lesser-known: under about $100 million a day before the event; not a mega-cap.

facts.quote: No prior advance is required. The HVE is often the first day of a new story
facts.claim: No prior advance is required; the HVE often starts a new story.

facts.quote: The close sits in the upper half of the day's range (DCR 0.5 or more); 0.7 or more preferred. A grade cue, not a hard line.
facts.claim: The close in the upper half of the range is a grade cue, not a hard line.

facts.claim: The opening gap is a cue, not a rule.

facts.quote: A cue, not a rule: a group or theme setting volume records on the same day helps.
facts.claim: A group setting records the same day is a cue, not a rule.

facts.claim: No 10, 21 or 50-day requirement.

facts.quote: Rank the volume, not the gap. An earnings gap on big but ordinary volume in a well-owned name is a PEG

facts.quote: the HVE waits for day 2 to dip under the record day's close and reclaim it, with the day-2 low as the stop.
facts.claim: The HVE waits for the day-2 dip and reclaim.

facts.claim: A record-volume down day is never an HVE.

facts.claim: A named mistake: a 3x day on a mega-cap is an HVC, not an HVE.

facts.quote: Shorting a down-close record day because the app called it bearish.
facts.claim: A named mistake: shorting a down-close record day.

facts.claim: A+: a lesser-known name, small dollar volume before.

facts.quote: Green market: full risk. Yellow: smaller and fewer. Orange: A+ only. Red: mostly cash and shorts.
facts.claim: Green full risk, Yellow smaller, Orange A+ only, Red mostly cash.

facts.claim: No new buy in the 3 sessions before a report; it binds the later entries.

facts.claim: A gap through the stop: the first 30-minute low is the new stop; out past 2R.

facts.claim: A real stop order with the broker; it only moves up.

facts.claim: Under 1R after 10 trading days, sell.

facts.claim: Sell a big part into a climax run on your own long.

questions.q: On a High Volume Edge, what is the HVC?
questions.why: The record day's close. The HVC is a level you mark with a ray and an AVWAP, and keep for months.
questions.lesson_line: The HVC is the record day's close. That is the line.

wrong.The record day's high: The high is not the level. The card marks the close.
wrong.The record day's low: The low matters later, for the level. The HVC itself is the close.
wrong.The next day's open: Day 2's open is where the trigger starts. The level is the record day's close.

questions.q: A High Volume Edge is an up day: the record day closes over the prior close.
questions.why: True. An up close, and long only. A record-volume day that closes down is not this setup.
questions.lesson_line: Record volume and an up close. Both, or it is not an HVE.

questions.q: When is the taught High Volume Edge buy?
choices: A week later, on a pullback
questions.why: Day 2, the next session. The taught trigger is the one session after the record day. Not the record day's close, not a later day.
questions.lesson_line: The record day marks the level. Day 2 gives the trade.

wrong.At the record day's close: The close is the level, not the buy. The taught trigger waits for day 2.
wrong.At the record day's open: That is the Episodic Pivot's day: bought on the gap day itself. The HVE waits a session.
wrong.A week later, on a pullback: Later entries exist, each with its own trigger. The taught one is the very next session.

questions.q: On the day-2 entry the stop goes a few cents under the day-2 low.
questions.why: True. A few cents under the day-2 low, the low made before the reclaim. Not exactly on it.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first: a few cents under the day-2 low.

questions.q: Tap the words that fit the blank.
questions.sentence: Draw a ray at the HVC and an ___ from the record day.
questions.why: An anchored VWAP. A ray at the HVC and an AVWAP from the record day, kept for months. Shannon anchors at meaningful market events.
questions.lesson_line: Two marks on the chart: a ray at the close, an AVWAP from the day.

questions.q: A record-volume day on the monthly options expiry, the third Friday, can count as a High Volume Edge.
questions.why: False. Never the monthly options expiry, and never a month's last session. That volume is not demand.
questions.lesson_line: Check the calendar before the volume. Expiry and month-end do not count.

questions.q: Day 2 opens under the HVC and trades lower. What is the trigger?
choices: A trade back over the HVC
A trade over the record day's high
questions.answer: A trade back over the HVC
questions.why: A trade back over the HVC. Red to green through it: buy at market, a cent over the HVC, the moment it trades back over.
questions.lesson_line: Under, then back over the HVC. That is the trigger.

wrong.A close over the HVC: The trigger is intraday. Entries are market orders the moment it trades back over.
wrong.A trade over the record day's high: The line is the HVC, the record day's close, not its high.
wrong.A new low that holds: A low is where the stop goes. The trigger is the trade back over the HVC.

questions.q: The HVC itself is a good place for the High Volume Edge stop.
questions.why: False. The HVC is never the stop. Price trades under it in 98% of cases within 60 sessions.
questions.lesson_line: The HVC is a level to watch, not a stop to sit on.

questions.q: Which story fits a High Volume Edge?
choices: A trial win in a quiet stock
The last session of a quarter
questions.answer: A trial win in a quiet stock
questions.why: A trial result in a quiet stock. A fresh story arrives all at once. An ordinary beat on big volume is a PEG.
questions.lesson_line: Ask what changed. A new story makes an HVE; a routine beat does not.

wrong.An ordinary earnings beat: Earnings on ordinary big volume is a PEG, not an HVE.
wrong.A monthly options expiry rally: Expiry volume is not demand. The card rules that day out.
wrong.The last session of a quarter: Month-end volume is not demand. The card rules it out.

questions.q: A High Volume Edge needs a prior advance of 30% or more before the record day.
questions.why: False. No prior advance is required. The HVE is often the first day of a new story.
questions.lesson_line: No run-up needed. The record day is often the start.

questions.q: Day 2 opens over the HVC and never trades under it. Is that our trigger?
choices: No; it needs a close over
questions.why: No. Day 2 must open at or under the HVC and trade under it. One that never dips is not this trigger; it may become a later entry.
questions.lesson_line: No dip under the HVC, no day-2 trade.

wrong.Yes; it is holding above: Strength is not the trigger here. The trigger is under, then back over.
wrong.Yes; buy the open: Buying the open over the HVC is not our trade. Day 2 has to dip and reclaim.
wrong.No; it needs a close over: No close is needed. The trigger is an intraday trade back over the HVC.

questions.q: On big enough news we buy a High Volume Edge pre-market, as Bonde does.
questions.why: False. No buys outside regular trading hours. Bonde enters pre-market or at the open; we do not.
questions.lesson_line: Regular hours only. The news can wait for the bell.

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Never buy a High Volume Edge more than ___ over the HVC.
questions.why: 4%. No buy more than 4% over the HVC; the HVC is the buy point. A market order a cent over cannot breach it.
questions.lesson_line: The HVC is the buy point. Past 4% over it, you are chasing.

questions.q: When price closes under the HVC, the level is broken and comes off the chart.
questions.why: False. Trading or closing under the HVC is not an invalidation of the level. Do not erase it.
questions.lesson_line: Under the HVC is normal. Keep the line on the chart.

questions.q: Which name fits a High Volume Edge best?
questions.why: A thinly owned small company. The card wants a lesser-known stock, not a mega-cap. Bonde: widely covered names do not do as well.
questions.lesson_line: The less known the name, the bigger the new story.

wrong.A mega-cap everyone owns: Not a mega-cap. A big day there is usually just an HVC.
wrong.A widely covered large cap: Bonde: earnings breakouts in widely covered companies do not do as well.

questions.q: When a High Volume Edge works, you add to it on the first pullback to the HVC.
questions.why: False. Full size at one price with one stop; no adding. A later setup at the level is a new trade, not an add.
questions.lesson_line: One price, one stop, one size. No adds.

questions.q: What is it?
questions.story: A stock trades the most shares in its history. It closes down 15% on the day.
choices: Not an HVE; it closed down
An HVE; record volume is enough
questions.answer: Not an HVE; it closed down
questions.why: Not an HVE. A record-volume day that closed down is never an HVE, and we trade this setup long only. Shorting it is a named mistake.
questions.lesson_line: Check the colour of the record bar first.

wrong.An HVE short: We trade the HVE long only. Shorting a down-close record day is a named mistake.
wrong.An HVE; record volume is enough: Record volume is half of it. The day must close up.

questions.q: A later entry at the HVC sets up two sessions before the next report. Our rule?
choices: No new buy before the report
Buy; the HVC is strong support
questions.answer: No new buy before the report
questions.why: No new buy. No new buy in the 3 sessions before an earnings report. It binds the later entries.
questions.lesson_line: Three sessions before a report, no new buys.

wrong.Buy half size: Size does not fix it. The rule is no new buy in that window.
wrong.Buy; the HVC is strong support: The level does not lift the rule. No buy in the 3 sessions before a report.
wrong.Buy with a wider stop: The stop is never widened, and the window still says no.

questions.q: Bought at 56.28 with the stop at 55.53. Where is 3R?
questions.why: 58.53. Three times the risk, added to the buy. A third comes off there.
questions.lesson_line: Sell a third at 3R. Know the price before the buy.

questions.q: On a High Volume Edge winner the stop stays at the day-2 low until the last third is sold.
questions.why: False. The stop moves to breakeven between 2R and 5R, at the first trim by default. It only moves up.
questions.lesson_line: At the first trim, the stop goes to breakeven.

questions.q: The market reading is Orange. Which High Volume Edge trades may you take?
questions.why: Only A+ setups. Green, full risk; Yellow, smaller and fewer; Orange, only A+; Red, mostly cash and shorts.
questions.lesson_line: The market sets how much you play.

wrong.Any HVE, full size: Full risk is Green. Orange is A+ only.
wrong.None at all: That is closer to Red. Orange still allows A+ setups.
wrong.Any HVE, half size: Smaller and fewer is Yellow. Orange is A+ only.

questions.q: Buy or pass?
questions.story: The HVC is 20.00. Day 2 dipped to 19.40 and reclaimed it while you were away. It now trades 21.10.
choices: Pass; it is 5.5% over the HVC
Buy; it reclaimed the HVC level
Buy half; it is close enough
questions.answer: Pass; it is 5.5% over the HVC
questions.why: Pass. 21.10 is 5.5% over the HVC, past the 4% chase limit. Chasing costs size: the stop stays put and the distance grows.
questions.lesson_line: Missed the reclaim: let it go, or wait for a later setup at the level.

wrong.Buy; it reclaimed the HVC level: The reclaim was the trigger. It is now past 4% over the buy point.
wrong.Buy half; it is close enough: Half size does not cure a chase. Past 4% is a pass.
wrong.Buy with the stop at 20.00: A different stop does not cure a chase. Past 4% over the HVC is a pass.

questions.q: Ten trading days after your day-2 buy the trade sits at 0.6R. Our rule?
choices: Hold; the level is still there
Add to it at the HVC
questions.why: Sell it. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, freeing the money.
questions.lesson_line: Ten days and under 1R: let it go.

wrong.Hold; the level is still there: The level stays on the chart. The trade still goes after 10 days under 1R.
wrong.Add to it at the HVC: No adding, and a dead trade is sold.
wrong.Move the stop to breakeven: Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R. At 0.6R after 10 days the time stop applies.

questions.q: Tap the words that fit the blank.
questions.sentence: On the day-2 buy, place a real ___ with the broker.
questions.why: A stop order. Every position has a real stop order with the broker, not a stop kept in your head. It only moves up.
questions.lesson_line: The stop lives with the broker, not in your head.

questions.q: Fill 58.13. The day-2 low is 57.56 and the stop sits two cents under it. How far below the fill is the stop, in percent?
questions.why: 1.01%. Two cents under the day-2 low is 57.54, VRTX's stop in May 2012.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, distance second, size last.

questions.q: After the event the stock trades 3,000,000 shares a day on average. The most shares you may own?
questions.why: 30,000 shares. Never more than 1% of the average daily volume, measured on the post-event average.
questions.lesson_line: Own no more than 1% of a day's volume.

questions.q: Bought at 84.90, stop 83.38. The stock trades 92.50. How many R is that?
questions.why: 5.0R. Another third comes off at 5R, after the first third at 3R. Then trail the last third.
questions.lesson_line: 3R a third, 5R a third, trail the rest.

questions.q: Before the record day the stock traded 1,200,000 shares a day at 11.50. How many dollars a day is that?
questions.why: $13.8 million a day. Well under about $100 million: a lesser-known name, the card's grade cue.
questions.lesson_line: Read the dollar volume before the day. Small means lesser-known.

questions.q: HVE or something else?
questions.story: A widely owned stock gaps up on earnings and closes 28.1% higher. Volume tops the past year but barely beats the old high. Day 2 dips and reclaims the close.
choices: A PEG; big but ordinary volume
An HVE; the gap is big
questions.answer: A PEG; big but ordinary volume
questions.why: A PEG. An earnings gap on big but ordinary volume in a well-owned name is a PEG, not an HVE. ROKU, taken as an HVE, was stopped at 0.0R.
questions.lesson_line: Rank the volume, not the gap.

wrong.An HVE; the reclaim triggers: The trigger is fine. The record day is not an HVE: the volume is ordinary for this name.
wrong.An HVE; the gap is big: The gap does not make it. Rank the volume, not the gap.
wrong.An Episodic Pivot: An EP is bought on the gap day itself over the opening-range high. Day 2 is past that.

questions.q: What is the trade on day 2?
questions.story: A stock rises 29% on the most shares it has ever traded and closes near the high. Day 2 opens 2.1% over that close. Its low stays 1.7% above it.
choices: No trigger; it never dipped under
Buy the open; strength is the tell
Short it; the gap will fill
questions.answer: No trigger; it never dipped under
questions.why: No trigger. Day 2 opened 2.1% over the HVC and its low stayed 1.7% over it. A valid HVE day, no day-2 trade.
questions.lesson_line: A strong day 2 is not our trigger. Wait for a later setup at the level.

wrong.Buy the open; strength is the tell: Our trigger needs a dip under the HVC first. This one never dipped.
wrong.Buy, stop under the HVC: The HVC is never the stop, and there was no trigger.
wrong.Short it; the gap will fill: We trade the HVE long only.

questions.q: What do you do?
questions.story: The HVC is 13.11. Day 2 opens at 12.80 and trades lower. Midday it trades back up to 13.12.
choices: Buy at market, a cent over
questions.answer: Buy at market, a cent over
questions.why: Buy at market, a cent over the HVC. Red to green through the HVC is the trigger, and entries are market orders.
questions.lesson_line: Set the alert at the HVC. When it trades back over, buy at market.

wrong.Wait for a close over 13.11: The trigger is intraday, the moment it trades back over.
wrong.Place a limit at 12.80: Entries are market orders, and 12.80 is under the trigger.
wrong.Wait for a new high: The line is the HVC. A new high comes later and past the chase limit.

questions.q: Start or climax?
questions.story: The stock is on its fourth straight up day, each one gapping higher. Today it trades record volume and closes up 25%.
questions.why: A climax. Not on the third to fifth day of a straight-up burst, and not after a 60% run in 60 sessions. A record day there is often the end.
questions.lesson_line: A record at the start is a beginning. A record at the end of a burst is a climax.

wrong.A start; plan day 2: Not on the third to fifth day of a straight-up burst. This is the fourth.
wrong.A start; buy the close: The close is not our buy, and this day is a climax.

questions.q: If the stock gaps under your stop, the first 30-minute low is the new stop, unless that takes the loss past 2R.
questions.why: True. The gap rule: the first 30 minutes of the gap-down day decide. Past 2R, get out.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through the stop: the first 30 minutes set the new stop.

questions.q: What do you do at the open?
questions.story: Your High Volume Edge long closed at 2.7R. The next morning it gaps open at 3.5R.
choices: Sell a third at the open
Move the stop up and hold
questions.answer: Sell a third at the open
questions.why: Sell a third at the open. If a stock opens above a trim level, take that trim at the open.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through a trim level is the trim. Take it at the open.

wrong.Wait for the close: The level is already passed. Waiting gives the gap a chance to fill.
wrong.Sell everything: A third at 3R. The rest waits for 5R and the trail.
wrong.Move the stop up and hold: The stop moves up too, but the trim is the rule at the open.

questions.q: The record day closed under the 200-day. Day 2's fill is above it. Does it qualify?
choices: Yes; the trade is above it
No; the record day was under
Only after a week above it
questions.answer: Yes; the trade is above it
questions.why: Yes. The trade, not the HVE day, must be above the 200-day at the moment of entry. No longs below the 200-day.
questions.lesson_line: Judge the 200-day at the fill, not on the record day.

wrong.No; the record day was under: The record day does not decide. The fill does.
wrong.Only after a week above it: No wait is in the rule. The fill above the 200-day qualifies.

questions.q: Which record-volume up day never counts as a High Volume Edge?
choices: The last session of a month
A day after a trial result
A day in a beaten-down stock
questions.answer: The last session of a month
questions.why: The last session of a month. Month-end and the monthly options expiry are ruled out: the volume is not demand.
questions.lesson_line: Month-end volume is bookkeeping, not buyers.

wrong.A day after a trial result: A trial result is a fresh story, the kind the card wants.
wrong.A day with a 30% gap: A gap is a cue, not a bar. It does not rule the day out.
wrong.A day in a beaten-down stock: Beaten-down is often where it starts. No prior trend is needed.

questions.q: What do you do?
questions.story: Six sessions after your day-2 buy the stock closes 2% under the HVC. Your stop under the day-2 low has not traded.
questions.why: Hold. Closing under the HVC is not an invalidation of the level, and the stop is the exit. It has not traded.
questions.lesson_line: Under the HVC is normal. The stop, not the line, ends the trade.

wrong.Sell; the level failed: A close under the HVC is not a failure. Price trades under it most of the time.
wrong.Erase the level; it broke: Do not erase it. The level stays on the chart for months.
wrong.Widen the stop for room: The stop only moves up, never wider.

questions.q: What is the HVC now?
questions.story: You bought day 2 at 55.46 with a stop at 53.73. It traded two sessions later, a planned loss. Weeks on, the stock closes under the record day's low.
questions.why: Overhead. A close under the record day's low ends the level as support. QGEN slid to 38.80, under its 46.07 low.
questions.lesson_line: Under the record day's low, the HVC turns from floor to ceiling.

wrong.Support; buy it again: Under the record day's low it is no longer support. A new buy needs a new trigger.
wrong.Gone; erase it: Keep it on the chart. It now sits overhead.
wrong.The new stop level: You are out already. The line now marks overhead supply.

questions.q: Was the stop a mistake?
questions.story: You bought day 2 at 80.07, stop 77.24. The next session takes your stop, and within three sessions the low is 71.08. Weeks later it runs to 88.84.
choices: No; the stop is the exit
Yes; it needed a wider stop
questions.answer: No; the stop is the exit
questions.why: No. The stop is the exit, and you followed the plan. A shake-out that later runs is the cost of a tight stop, not a reason to widen it.
questions.lesson_line: A loss taken at plan is the system working.

wrong.Yes; it needed a wider stop: The stop only moves up. It then collapsed to 56.05, so room would have cost more.
wrong.Yes; you should have held: Holding past the stop is not in the plan. The stop is the exit.

questions.q: Buy it back?
questions.story: Stopped out the day after your day-2 buy, you watch the stock grind back up. It runs to 88.84 with no new day-2 trigger and no setup at the level.
choices: Yes; it is back over the HVC
Yes; the old stop proved right
questions.why: Only on a new trigger. After a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade. Each later entry has its own trigger and stop.
questions.lesson_line: Stopped out: the next trade needs its own trigger.

wrong.Yes; it is back over the HVC: Being over the HVC is not a trigger. The new trade needs its own setup.
wrong.Yes; the old stop proved right: That is chasing the past. A re-entry needs a fresh trigger and stop.
wrong.Never; the stock failed you: Not never. A new trigger is a new trade with its own stop.

questions.q: Your High Volume Edge long runs four straight days, each gapping higher on rising volume. Our rule?
choices: Sell a big part into it
Move the stop to the HVC
questions.answer: Sell a big part into it
questions.why: Sell a big part into it. A climax run on your own long: sell a big part into it, a judgment call.
questions.lesson_line: A burst on your own long is a gift. Sell into it.

wrong.Add on the next gap: No adding, and a burst is a place to sell.
wrong.Hold all for the trail: A climax is the exception. Sell a big part into it.
wrong.Move the stop to the HVC: The HVC is never the stop. Sell into the burst instead.

questions.q: After day 2, which is a follow-up entry at the HVC?
choices: An Oops Reversal at the HVC
questions.answer: An Oops Reversal at the HVC
questions.why: An Oops Reversal at the HVC. The follow-up entries are our own setups at the level, each with its own trigger and stop.
questions.lesson_line: The level keeps paying. Each later entry is its own setup.

wrong.Any touch of the HVC: A touch is not a trigger. The later entries are named setups.
wrong.Averaging down at the HVC: No adding. Each later entry is a new trade with its own stop.
wrong.The first close under it: A close under the HVC is no buy signal. It is not even an invalidation.

questions.q: Which grades higher?
questions.story: Two stocks set lifetime volume records on fresh news, both up big. One traded $14 million a day before. The other traded $3 billion.
questions.why: The $14 million name. The card's A+ is a lesser-known name with small dollar volume before the day. A mega-cap or well-owned large cap is B- at best.
questions.lesson_line: The quieter the name before, the louder the record.

wrong.The $3 billion name: A well-owned large cap grades down. The card cut names like that.
wrong.They grade the same: Dollar volume before the day is a grade cue. Small is A+.

questions.q: Can it still be a High Volume Edge?
questions.story: An earnings report sends a stock up 22%. It trades more shares than on any day in its history, far beyond its usual volume.
choices: No; it is always a PEG
questions.why: Yes. Earnings so big the volume is extreme can be an HVE. DOCU's record was all-time, so it is an HVE, not a PEG.
questions.lesson_line: Earnings can count. The volume decides, not the report.

wrong.No; earnings days never count: Earnings can count when the volume is extreme.
wrong.No; it is always a PEG: A PEG is ordinary big volume. An all-time record is not ordinary.

questions.q: How does the group read?
questions.story: Four names in one theme all set volume records on the same day. One gives a clean day-2 reclaim of its HVC.
choices: It helps; a cue, not a rule
A rule; all four must trigger
A warning; it is a crowd
questions.answer: It helps; a cue, not a rule
questions.why: It helps. A group or theme setting volume records the same day helps. It is a cue, not a rule.
questions.lesson_line: A group moving together is a tailwind, not a trigger.

wrong.A rule; all four must trigger: The group is a cue. Each trade still needs its own trigger.
wrong.A warning; it is a crowd: The card reads a group record as a help, not a warning.

questions.q: Account 40,000. Risk 0.5%. Fill 20.18, stop 19.89. How many shares?
questions.why: 689 shares. Account times risk, divided by the stop distance, rounded down. Then check the position cap.
questions.lesson_line: The stop sets the size, never the other way round.

questions.q: A trade under the record day's low ends the level as support, even if the day closes back above it.
questions.why: False. A close under the record day's low ends it as support. A trade under it that closes back above does not.
questions.lesson_line: The level ends on a close under the record day's low.

questions.q: Where is the stop now?
questions.story: Your High Volume Edge long: buy 50.00, stop 48.50. It gaps open at 47.90. The first 30-minute bar's low is 47.40.
questions.why: 47.40. On a gap through the stop, the first 30-minute low is the new stop. The loss there stays inside 2R, so you hold to it.
questions.lesson_line: Let the first 30 minutes set the stop on a gap against you.

wrong.Out at the open, 47.90: The gap rule waits for the first 30 minutes, unless the loss passes 2R.
wrong.Back at 48.50, the old stop: Price already gapped through it. The first 30-minute low sets the new stop.
wrong.46.00, for more room: Room is not a rule. The first 30-minute low is the stop.

questions.q: Gap Support and the High Volume Edge both mark a big up day. Which line does Gap Support defend?
questions.why: The gap-up day's low. Gap Support defends that low days or weeks later; the HVE's line is the record day's close.
questions.lesson_line: Find the line: Gap Support, the gap day's low; HVE, the record day's close.

wrong.The record day's close: That is the HVE's line, the HVC. Gap Support uses the gap day's low.
wrong.The gap-up day's high: The high is not either setup's line.
wrong.The prior day's close: That is the line red to green uses. Gap Support defends the gap day's low.

questions.q: Inside our rules, what would have saved it?
questions.story: You bought day 2 at 331.66, stop 323.98. The next day it reaches 2.3R. Four sessions after the buy, the low trades 322.50 and takes the stop.
questions.why: Stop to breakeven at 2R. Our rule moves it between 2R and 5R; moved at 2R, this loss is a scratch. Left for the first trim, it is a planned loss.
questions.lesson_line: A 2R gain given back is a scratch once the stop sits at breakeven.

wrong.A stop under 320 for room: The stop only moves up, never wider.
wrong.Selling it all at 2R: Our first trim is a third at 3R, not everything at 2R.
wrong.Skipping the day-2 trigger: The trigger was valid. The breakeven move is the tool.

questions.q: Which is the one thing you never do?
questions.story: The HVC is 13.11. Day 2 opens 12.80, falls well lower, then reclaims 13.11. The honest stop under the day-2 low is far wider than your plan allows.
choices: Pull the stop in to fit
Skip and wait for a later setup
Size down from the real stop
questions.answer: Pull the stop in to fit
questions.why: Pull the stop in. If the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade. NAVN's honest day-2 stop was 7.5% wide; a later entry at the level was the plan.
questions.lesson_line: Never move the stop to fit the size. Move the size, or skip.

wrong.Skip and wait for a later setup: That is the plan when the stop does not fit. Skip, then watch the level.
wrong.Size down from the real stop: Sizing from the real stop is the rule. Pulling it in is the mistake.

questions.q: By our rules, what kept this a win?
questions.story: Bought day 2 at 84.90, stop 83.38. 5R comes in two sessions; the peak is day 17. By day 30 it has round-tripped under the HVC.
questions.why: The thirds at 3R and 5R. INOD hit 5R in two sessions, peaked +47% on day 17, then round-tripped under the HVC by day 30.
questions.lesson_line: Trims bank the move. The trail decides the rest.

wrong.Holding all of it: Holding it all rides the round trip back under the HVC.
wrong.A stop at the HVC: The HVC is never the stop. The trims did the work.
wrong.Adding on day 17: No adding, and day 17 was the peak.

questions.q: Duncan exits on a close under the HVC; our High Volume Edge plan does the same.
questions.why: False. Duncan also exits on a close under the HVC. Ours: the stop is a few cents under the day-2 low, and under the HVC is not an invalidation.
questions.lesson_line: Our exit is the stop, not a close under the line.

questions.q: Does the 50-day rule it out?
questions.story: A beaten-down stock sets a lifetime volume record on fresh news and closes up, still under its 50-day. Day 2 reclaims the HVC above the 200-day.
choices: Yes; it must be over the 50-day
questions.why: No. The card has no 10, 21 or 50-day requirement on the HVE day. The 200-day is the line, and the fill is above it.
questions.lesson_line: The 200-day decides. The shorter averages do not.

wrong.Yes; it must be over the 50-day: No 50-day test applies on this card. The 200-day at the fill does.
wrong.Yes; the 50 must top the 200: That is a check for other setups. The HVE has no 50-day requirement.

questions.q: Does the flat open rule it out?
questions.story: A stock opens flat, then grinds higher all day on fresh news. It closes near the high on the most shares in its history.
choices: No; the gap is a cue, not a rule
Yes; an HVE must open with a gap
Yes; a flat open makes it an EP
questions.answer: No; the gap is a cue, not a rule
questions.why: No. The opening gap is a cue, not a rule. Some good HVEs gapped 3% or even 0.5%. The record volume and the up close carry it.
questions.lesson_line: Gap or no gap, a record up day can be an HVE.

wrong.Yes; an HVE must open with a gap: A gap helps the grade. It is not required.
wrong.Yes; a flat open makes it an EP: An EP needs the gap. A record up day without one is the HVE's lesson.

questions.q: How does it grade?
questions.story: Up 100% on 62 times its average volume, a lifetime record. But it closes at 0.26 of the day's range.
choices: Down; it closed low in range
A+; the volume is huge and rare
A+; up 100% is the whole story
questions.answer: Down; it closed low in range
questions.why: Down. A close in the lower half of a huge range grades B-. MBX closed at 0.26 of its range, a supply day dressed as an HVE.

wrong.A+; the volume is huge and rare: Volume is not the whole grade. The close tells who won the day.
wrong.A+; up 100% is the whole story: The move is big, the close is weak. The close grades it down.
wrong.No trade; it closed down: It closed up 100% on the day. The weak spot is where in the range.

questions.q: HVE or not?
questions.story: A mega-cap everyone owns trades its biggest volume in a year. That is about 3 times its average, and it closes up 7%.
choices: Not an HVE; just an HVC
questions.answer: Not an HVE; just an HVC
questions.why: Not an HVE. Calling any year-high volume an HVE is a named mistake: a 3x day on a mega-cap is an HVC.
questions.lesson_line: A big day in a mega-cap is an HVC, not an edge.

wrong.An HVE; a one-year record: A year-high on a mega-cap is not an HVE.
wrong.An HVE; it closed up: An up close is needed, not enough. The name and the size of the record fail.

questions.q: What happened, by the plan?
questions.story: An earnings record day. You buy day 2 at 48.34, stop 47.52, a real stop order with the broker. Day 3 opens 49.56 and reverses to 46.94.
choices: Still in; it closed over the HVC
A mistake; the stop was too tight
questions.why: Stopped, a small planned loss. The broker stop took it on the way through, as planned.
questions.lesson_line: A real stop order acts when you cannot. That is its job.

wrong.Still in; it closed over the HVC: Yesterday's close does not hold today. The stop traded at 47.52.
wrong.A mistake; the stop was too tight: Tight day-2 stops are the design. The first sessions decide the trade.

questions.q: Our High Volume Edge stop sits a set 3% to 5% under the HVC, as Duncan's does.
questions.why: False. Duncan's stop is 3% to 5% under the HVC. Ours is a few cents under the day-2 low, the low made before the reclaim.
questions.lesson_line: Our stop comes from the chart: the day-2 low, not a set percent.

questions.q: On a tight day-2 stop, 3R is often a few percent over the buy. The first trim is still a third at 3R.
questions.why: True. Because the stop is small, 3R is often only 3% to 7% over the buy. The hard rule is still a third at 3R.
questions.lesson_line: Read the percent, keep the rule: a third at 3R.

questions.q: What do you do?
questions.story: The market reading turns Red. A clean High Volume Edge gives its day-2 reclaim.
choices: Buy it, but at full size
Buy it, but at half size
questions.why: Pass. In a Red market: mostly cash and shorts. A clean HVE is still a long.
questions.lesson_line: Red market, mostly cash. The setup can wait.

wrong.Buy it, but at full size: Full risk is a Green market. Red is mostly cash.
wrong.Buy it, but at half size: Smaller and fewer is Yellow. Red is mostly cash and shorts.

questions.q: Hold through the report?
questions.story: Your High Volume Edge long is up 3.2R. The company reports in two days.
choices: Yes; move the stop to breakeven
questions.why: No. Hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R. At 3.2R, sell before it.
questions.lesson_line: Into a report, only a 5R cushion stays.

wrong.Yes; the level is strong: The level does not change the rule. Under 5R, sell before the report.
wrong.Yes; move the stop to breakeven: A stop cannot catch a gap. The rule is 5R or out.

questions.q: An AVWAP from the record day is the kind of anchor Shannon describes: fixed at a large price movement event.
questions.why: True. Shannon anchors from meaningful market events, such as a large price movement. Our AVWAP starts on the record day.
questions.lesson_line: Anchor the AVWAP where the story changed.

questions.q: Write the plan: entry, stop, first trim.
questions.story: A quiet stock trades record volume, up 37%, and closes near its high, 20.17. Day 2 dips under that close to a low of 19.91, then trades back through it.
choices: Buy the close, stop the record low
questions.why: 20.18, stop 19.89, a third at 3R. A market buy a cent over the HVC, the stop a few cents under the day-2 low. TVTX ran to +70% by day 54.
questions.lesson_line: Entry, stop, trim before the buy. Then let the plan work.

wrong.Buy the close, stop the record low: The close is not our buy, and the record day's low is not the day-2 stop.
wrong.Wait for 21, stop 19.89: The trigger is the trade back over the HVC, not a higher price.
wrong.20.18, stop at the HVC: The HVC is never the stop. It sits under the day-2 low.

questions.q: What is your first High Volume Edge buy?
questions.story: A trial result hits at 7 a.m. The stock trades far higher pre-market on huge volume and holds all day.
choices: Day 2, a reclaim of the HVC
The open, over the first high
questions.answer: Day 2, a reclaim of the HVC
questions.why: Day 2, a reclaim of the HVC. No buys outside regular hours, and the taught trigger is day 2, not the record day.
questions.lesson_line: The news sets the level. Day 2 sets the trade.

wrong.The open, over the first high: That is the Episodic Pivot's entry on the gap day. Ours waits for day 2.
wrong.The record day's close: The close is the level, not the buy.

questions.q: Hidden ticker, the last bar is the record day. Plan the day-2 trade or pass?
choices: Pass; a climax after a run
questions.why: Plan day 2. A flat line for six months, 16% under its 200-day, then a 126% gap on 18x volume, an all-time record. The HVC was never traded again; +68% by day 59.
questions.lesson_line: A quiet stock, a new story, record volume: mark the close and plan day 2.

wrong.Pass; a climax after a run: There was no run before it. Six flat months, then the record day.
wrong.Pass; it is under the 200-day: The record day closed far above it. The fill on day 2 is what counts.

questions.q: Hidden ticker, the last bar is a record-volume day. Plan the day-2 trade or pass?
choices: Pass; a climax after a long run
Plan day 2; it is record volume
Plan day 2; it doubled in price
questions.answer: Pass; a climax after a long run
questions.why: Pass. The close before the record day was 72.5% over its 60-session low. A climax, not a start: day 2 triggered, was stopped at 0.0R, and it topped within two months.
questions.lesson_line: Look left before you mark the level. A record after a big run is a climax.

wrong.Plan day 2; it is record volume: Record volume after a 60% run in 60 sessions is a climax, not our start.
wrong.Plan day 2; it doubled in price: The size of the day does not fix the run before it.

questions.q: What do you do?
questions.story: A record day closes at 45.00. Day 2 opens 44.20, trades to 43.60 and closes 44.00, never back over 45.00. You are flat.
questions.why: Nothing. Day 2 never trades back over the HVC: no trigger. The level stays on the chart for a later setup.
questions.lesson_line: No setup, no trade. Keep the line and wait.

wrong.Buy the close at 44.00: No trigger came. The buy is a trade back over the HVC.
wrong.Buy, stop under 43.60: A stop needs a trigger first. There was none.
wrong.Erase the level: Keep it. Later setups form at the level.
